source_version: Capella (continuously deployed, no discrete version number)

concepts.label: Recurring Timer (self-rearming)
concepts.reused_or_minted: minted - there is no dedicated 'recurring Timer' API; a Timer callback recreates a new one-shot eventing:timer for itself every time it fires, so recurrence is a hand-written self-rearm loop built on the one-shot Timer primitive, not a distinct scheduler construct

relations.subject: eventing:control-document
relations.evidence: The Timer callback function relies on a control document which, if mutated, controls whether a recurring Timer is created or cancelled.

relations.subject: eventing:timer-callback
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: minted - verb phrase for a Timer callback that creates a new Timer referencing itself before or while doing its own work, producing indefinite recurrence out of the one-shot Timer primitive
relations.evidence:
Re-executes the timer ASAP to ensure the Timer keeps running in case  
    // errors or script timeouts happen in later "recurring work"

relations.subject: eventing:control-document
relations.evidence: This has no effect if the Timer created has already fired.

relations.subject: eventing:recurring-timer-pattern
relations.evidence: If `active` is true, the Eventing Function creates a series of Timers that fire 30 seconds into the future. If `active` is false, the Eventing Function cancels any existing Timers.

notable_absence.finding: The rearm call happens at the top of the callback ('Re-executes the timer ASAP') specifically so the recurrence survives errors or script timeouts in the callback's own later logic - meaning the recurring-Timer pattern is explicitly documented as best-effort/self-healing against callback failure, not as a guaranteed periodic scheduler; there is no retry-count limit, backoff, or failure-alerting concept associated with it.
